copula.rule_a2: English always needs am / is / are. 'I geologist' needs 'am'.
copula.rule_b1: English never drops the verb 'to be': every sentence needs it, even when Mongolian would omit it.
copula.bridge: Монголоор 'Би геологич' гэж хэлдэг — үйл үг хэрэггүй. Англиар 'am' заавал хэрэгтэй. (Mongolian drops the linking verb; English cannot.)

examples.explanation: English never drops 'to be': add is — and the article with it.
No verb in the sentence → add am/is/are.

lesson.explain_b1: English never drops the verb "to be". Mongolian says "Би багш" — two words, no verb — and it is a complete sentence. English cannot do this: every sentence needs a verb, so you must add am/is/are. Notice that "I am a teacher" needs TWO additions: the verb "am" AND the article "a". This one four-word sentence contains the two biggest differences between your languages.
lesson.explain_a2: Монголоор "Би багш" гэж хэлдэг — үйл үг хэрэггүй. Англиар үйл үг ЗААВАЛ хэрэгтэй: I am a teacher. "Am" болон "a" хоёуланг нь нэм.

extra_examples.right: My office is small but warm.

how: Read your sentence. Where is the verb? No verb → add am/is/are.
I → am · he/she/it/нэг юм → is · you/we/they/олон → are.
Past: was (ганц тоо) / were (олон тоо).
lesson.watch_out: Questions with 'be' flip the order and need NO do: "Is she happy?" — never "Does she is happy?"
lesson.tip: Present forms: I am · he/she/it is · you/we/they are. Past: was/were.

word_order.rule_a2: English order: person, then action, then thing. I analysed the samples.
word_order.rule_b1: Mongolian builds backwards (SOV); English builds forwards (SVO). The verb comes before its object.
word_order.bridge: Би ном уншсан = I book read. One rule covers five error types: Mongolian builds backwards; English builds forwards.

examples.wrong: We drilled last week three holes.
examples.right: We drilled three holes last week.
examples.explanation: Time words go at the end (or the very start), not in the middle.
Pronouns go INSIDE a phrasal verb: turn it on.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian builds backwards; English builds forwards. In Mongolian everything that describes something comes BEFORE it, and the verb comes last: Би ном уншсан (I book read). English is the opposite: the verb comes right after the person, and descriptions usually come after the thing. One rule — subject, then verb, then object — fixes five different error types at once, so learn the principle, not five separate rules.
lesson.explain_a2: Монгол хэл арагшаа барьдаг, англи хэл урагшаа барьдаг. Дараалал: ХЭН + ЮУ ХИЙСЭН + ЮУГ. I read a book.

extra_examples.wrong: We last week my parents visited.
extra_examples.right: We visited my parents last week.

how: Start with WHO (the subject).
The verb comes SECOND — immediately after who.
Then WHAT, then where, then when: I read the report at home yesterday.
lesson.watch_out: Never put anything between the verb and its object — that slot is welded shut in English.
lesson.tip: Basic shape: WHO + ACTION + WHAT (+ where + when). Time words go at the end or the very beginning — never in the middle.

articles.rule_a2: Almost every single thing-word needs 'a', 'an' or 'the' in front.
articles.rule_b1: A singular countable noun needs an article: 'a/an' for new or general, 'the' for one both people know.
articles.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

examples.explanation: Job words need 'an' before a vowel sound: an engineer.

examples.right: I work in the mining industry.
examples.explanation: Industry names take 'the': the mining industry.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian has no articles — but it DOES mark definiteness, with the accusative suffix -ыг/-ийг on specific objects. So you already have the concept; English just uses a separate word in front instead of a suffix behind. Use "a/an" for something new or general ("we found a nice café"), "the" for something both people know ("the café we found"), and nothing for general plurals and most names ("apples", "Mongolia"). "An" goes before a vowel SOUND: an hour, but a university.
lesson.explain_a2: "Ном уншсан" (ямар ч ном) = a book. "Номыг уншсан" (тодорхой ном) = the book. -ыг гэдэг дагаврыг та мэднэ — англид "the" гэдэг үг урд нь ордог.

extra_examples.wrong: I saw a rock. A rock was heavy.
extra_examples.right: I saw a rock. The rock was heavy.

how: Singular thing, new or general → a/an: a café, an idea.
Both people know WHICH one → the: the café we found.
General plurals and names → nothing: apples, Mongolia, English.
a or an? Listen to the SOUND: an hour, but a university.
lesson.watch_out: The second mention flips to 'the': I saw a film. THE film was long.
lesson.tip: Second mention becomes "the": a rock … the rock. Languages and countries take no article.

verb_agreement.rule_a2: HE, SHE, IT adds -s: he works, she lives, it takes.
verb_agreement.rule_b1: Present-simple verbs take -s with a third-person singular subject. Mongolian verbs never change for person, so this must become a reflex.
verb_agreement.bridge: Монгол үйл үг хэн үйлдэхээс хамаарч өөрчлөгддөггүй. Англид зөвхөн he/she/it дээр -s нэмэгдэнэ.

examples.explanation: he/she/it + doesn't (not don't).
One person → verb + s: my father driveS.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian verbs never change for WHO does the action — English verbs change in exactly one place: he/she/it adds -s in the present simple. "I work, you work, they work — but he workS." This is the most common error in English learning worldwide, and knowing the rule is not enough: it must become a reflex through repetition, because you will always be too busy thinking about your message to compute it.
lesson.explain_a2: HE, SHE, IT → үйл үг дээр -s нэм: he works, she lives, it takes. Би, та, тэд нар → -s хэрэггүй.

extra_examples.wrong: My sister work in a bank.
extra_examples.right: My sister works in a bank.

extra_examples.wrong: It rain a lot in July.
extra_examples.right: It rains a lot in July.

how: Find the subject of the sentence.
he / she / it / one person / one thing → verb + s.
everyone, every X, my boss, the drill → also singular → + s.
I / you / we / they → no s.
lesson.watch_out: The negative moves the -s onto DO: he doesn't work (never "he don't" or "he doesn't works").
lesson.tip: Chant it — "HE-SHE-IT adds S." It sounds childish. It works.

plurals.rule_a2: After 2, 3, 4… add -s: three samples. English repeats itself.
plurals.rule_b1: English marks the plural even after a numeral. It is redundant — Mongolian is more efficient here — but it is obligatory.
plurals.bridge: Гурван ном → three books. Монголд тоо нь олон тоог хэлчихдэг тул -s хэрэггүй; англи давхардуулдаг. Логикгүй ч хүлээн зөвшөөр.

examples.explanation: After a number, add -s: three samples. English repeats itself.
Number + unit before a noun stays singular: a 500-metre hole.

lesson.explain_b1: In Mongolian, plural marking is optional, and after a numeral it is normally dropped — гурван ном, because "three" already says it. English repeats itself: three bookS, many sampleS, even when the number makes it obvious. This is not logical; it is simply obligatory. The one exception pattern: a number USED AS A DESCRIPTION stays singular — "a 500-metre road", "a three-day trip".
lesson.explain_a2: Гурван ном = three bookS. Англи хэл давхардуулдаг: тоо байсан ч -s заавал нэм. Логикгүй ч дүрэм ийм.
how: Any number above one → noun + s: three tickets.
many / several / a few → + s too.
Number used as a DESCRIPTION before a noun → singular: a three-day trip.
lesson.watch_out: Irregulars refuse -s: children, people, men, women, feet, teeth.
lesson.tip: After every number bigger than one: -s. Before a noun ("500-metre road"): no -s.

missing_subject.rule_a2: Every English sentence needs a subject. Use 'it' or 'there': It is raining. There are three samples.
missing_subject.rule_b1: English cannot tolerate a subjectless sentence, so it invents fake subjects: dummy 'it' and 'there'.
missing_subject.bridge: Монголоор өгүүлэгдэхүүнийг орхиж болно; англиар хэзээ ч болохгүй — 'it/there' гэсэн хиймэл өгүүлэгдэхүүн зохиодог.

examples.explanation: Weather, time and distance take the fake subject IT.
Nothing is raining — but English still needs a subject: IT.

lesson.explain_b1: English cannot tolerate a sentence without a subject — so it invents fake ones. Nothing is actually raining, but English says "IT is raining". Nothing is "there" in "THERE are three cups" — the word just fills the subject seat. Mongolian happily drops the subject when it is obvious; English never does. When your sentence has no natural subject, reach for "it" (weather, time, distance) or "there is/are" (existence).
lesson.explain_a2: Англи өгүүлбэрт эзэн ЗААВАЛ хэрэгтэй. "Бороо орж байна" → IT is raining. "Гурван аяга байна" → THERE are three cups.

extra_examples.wrong: Have three cups on the table.
extra_examples.right: There are three cups on the table.

extra_examples.wrong: Is important to check the data.
extra_examples.right: It is important to check the data.

how: Sentence has no natural doer? Don't start with the verb.
Weather / time / distance → IT: It is raining. It is late.
Something exists → THERE is/are: There are three cups.
lesson.watch_out: Match there is/are to the noun AFTER it: there IS a cup, there ARE three cups.
lesson.tip: Weather, time, distance → "it". Existence → "there is / there are".

topic_fronting.rule_a2: Don't start with 'About X'. Make X the subject: The report is late.
topic_fronting.rule_b1: English cannot announce a topic with 'about'. The best repair is to make the topic the subject of the sentence.
topic_fronting.bridge: «Тухай» бол нэр үгийн ард ордог дагавар үг. 'About the report, it is late' нь монгол бүтэц — англиар сэдвийг өгүүлэгдэхүүн болго: 'The report is late.'

examples.wrong: About the report, it is late.

examples.explanation: English can't announce a topic with 'about' — make it the subject.

examples.wrong: About my job, it is very busy.
examples.explanation: Delete 'About' and make the topic the subject.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian is a topic language: you announce what you are talking about, then comment on it — "Тайлангийн тухай — оройтсон". English cannot announce a topic with "about". The best repair is to make the topic the SUBJECT: "The report is late." Not "About the report, it is late." If you truly need a topic opener, "As for the report…" exists, but making the topic the subject is what native writing does.
lesson.explain_a2: "About X" гэж өгүүлбэр бүү эхэл. X-ийг өгүүлэгдэхүүн болго: "About the report, it is late" ❌ → "The report is late" ✅.

extra_examples.wrong: About my English, it is not good.
About the meeting, it was long.
About this phone, the price is high.
extra_examples.right: This phone has a high price.

how: Spot the pattern: your sentence starts with 'About X,'.
Delete 'About'.
Make X the subject and give it the verb: The report is late.
Occasional formal alternative: 'As for X, …' — but repair #1 is better.
lesson.watch_out: This habit returns every time you write about a NEW topic — that is normal, not failure. Re-apply the repair.
lesson.tip: See "About X, …" in your writing? Delete "About", make X the subject.

prepositions.rule_a2: Small words like at, in, on, to carry the meaning. Don't drop them: at 6:30, on Monday, in July.
prepositions.rule_b1: English prepositions do the job of Mongolian case suffixes. They are the grammar, not decoration — deleting one deletes the meaning.
prepositions.bridge: Монголоор нэр үгийн төгсгөл (-д, -аас, -тай) үүргийг заадаг. Англиар нэр үгийн ӨМНӨХ жижиг үг заадаг. Жижиг үгийг хаявал дагаврыг хаясантай адил.

examples.explanation: arrive AT a place: arrived at the site.
depends ON — learn verb + preposition as one chunk.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian marks a noun's role with a suffix on the end (-д, -аас, -тай); English marks it with a small word in FRONT (at, in, on, to, from, with). Those small words feel unimportant to a Mongolian ear — but they ARE the case system. Deleting "at" from "at 6:30" is like deleting -д from "зургаан цагт". Learn preposition + noun as one chunk: at night, on Monday, in July, at the airport.
lesson.explain_a2: -д, -аас, -тай гэдэг дагаврын ажлыг англид жижиг үгс хийдэг: at, in, on, to. Жижиг үгийг хаявал дагаврыг хаясантай адил.

extra_examples.right: We arrived at the airport at 8 o'clock.

how: Learn preposition + noun as ONE word: at-night, on-Monday, in-July.
Place ladder: AT a point → ON a surface → IN a space.
Time ladder: AT a clock time → ON a day → IN a month/year.
Verb pairs are chunks too: listen TO, depend ON, arrive AT.
lesson.watch_out: No preposition before next/last/every/each + time: next week, each day (never "in each day").
lesson.tip: Place ladder: AT a point (at the door) → ON a surface (on the table) → IN a space (in the office). Time: AT 6:30 → ON Monday → IN July.

questions_negation.rule_a2: Questions borrow 'do': Where do you work? Negatives too: I don't have time.
questions_negation.rule_b1: Find an auxiliary; if there is one, move it to the front; if not, borrow DO. Inside a longer sentence, a question becomes a statement again: tell me where it is.
questions_negation.bridge: Монголоор асуулт нь уу/үү гэсэн сүүл үгээр бүтдэг, үгийн дараалал өөрчлөгддөггүй. Англи 'do' гэдэг утгагүй туслах үг зээлдэг.

examples.explanation: Questions borrow 'do': Do you work here?
'Does' already carries the -s — the verb goes back to base form.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian makes a question with a particle at the end (уу/үү) and never changes word order. English inserts a helping verb instead — and one rule covers everything: find an auxiliary (am/is/can/have…); if there is one, move it to the front; if there is none, borrow DO. "You work here" has no auxiliary → "DO you work here?" The same DO carries negation: "I DON'T have time." And once a question sits inside a longer sentence it becomes a statement again: "Tell me where it IS", not "where is it".
lesson.explain_a2: Асуулт: DO/DOES-ийг урд нь тавь — Do you work here? Үгүйсгэл: don't/doesn't — I don't have time. Хоёр удаа үгүйсгэж болохгүй.

extra_examples.wrong: Tell me where is the bus stop.
extra_examples.right: Tell me where the bus stop is.

how: Look for an auxiliary: am/is/are/can/have/will…
Found one → move it in front of the subject: Can you swim?
None → borrow DO/DOES/DID: Do you work here?
Negation uses the same borrowed DO: I don't have time.
Question INSIDE a sentence → statement order returns: tell me where it IS.
lesson.watch_out: After does/did the main verb returns to base form: Does she work? (never "Does she works?").
lesson.tip: One rule: find the auxiliary → move it to the front → no auxiliary? borrow DO.

tense_aspect.rule_a2: since / for / already / yet / just → have + done: I have worked here since 2019.
tense_aspect.rule_b1: Past simple is a dot in the past; present perfect is an arrow touching today. Trigger words (since, for, already, yet, just, ever, never) cover 80% of uses. Stative verbs (know, want, need, like) never take -ing, and 'will' never follows 'if'.
tense_aspect.bridge: -сан нь өнгөрсөн ба одоотой холбоотой хоёуланг нь хэлдэг. Англи хоёрыг ялгадаг: цэг (worked) ба өнөөдрийг хүрсэн сум (have worked).

examples.explanation: 'Know' never takes -ing: I know.

examples.right: Yesterday I went to the site.
examples.explanation: 'Yesterday' = past, so the verb is past: went.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian -сан covers both "finished in the past" and "still matters now" — English splits them. Past simple is a DOT in the past: "I worked in Erdenet in 2019" (finished, disconnected). Present perfect is an ARROW touching today: "I have worked here since 2019" (still true). Seven trigger words choose the arrow about 80% of the time: since, for, already, yet, just, ever, never. Two more traps: stative verbs (know, want, need, like) never take -ing, and "will" never follows "if".
lesson.explain_a2: Дууссан үйл = цэг: I workED (2019 онд). Одоог хүртэл үргэлжилж байгаа = сум: I HAVE workED here since 2019. Түлхүүр үгс: since, for, already, yet, just.

extra_examples.wrong: If it will rain, we will stop.
extra_examples.right: If it rains, we will stop.

extra_examples.wrong: I already ate lunch, I eat at 12.
extra_examples.right: I have already eaten lunch — I ate at 12.

how: Finished and disconnected? → past simple (a dot): I worked there in 2019.
Started before, still true / matters now? → have + done (an arrow): I have worked here since 2019.
Trigger words choose the arrow: since, for, already, yet, just, ever, never.
After IF → present tense, never will: If it rains, we will stop.
lesson.watch_out: Stative verbs never take -ing: know, want, need, like, believe, understand — "I am knowing" is impossible.
lesson.tip: Draw the timeline: dot = past simple, arrow touching today = present perfect.

verb_form.rule_a2: After can/must/should: no 'to'. I can swim. After didn't: base form. I didn't go.
verb_form.rule_b1: Each slot fixes the verb form: modal + base (can go), did + base (didn't go), enjoy + -ing, look forward to + -ing, was/were + past participle (was written).
verb_form.bridge: Монгол нэг үгэнд дагавар давхарладаг; англи хэд хэдэн жижиг үгээр илэрхийлдэг тул хэлбэр нь хоорондоо таарах ёстой.

examples.explanation: 'Agree' is a verb, not an adjective: I agree.
have/has/had + gone (third form), never 'went'.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian stacks meaning into one word with suffixes; English spreads it across several small words — and each slot forces a verb form. After a modal: base form ("can swim", never "can to swim"). After did/didn't: base form ("didn't go", never "didn't went"). After have/has/had: third form ("have gone"). In the passive: third form ("was written"). After enjoy/finish/keep and after ANY preposition: -ing ("look forward to hearING").
lesson.explain_a2: can/must/should + үндсэн хэлбэр: can swim. didn't + үндсэн хэлбэр: didn't go. have + 3-р хэлбэр: have gone.

extra_examples.wrong: I finished to clean the kitchen.

how: After can/must/should → base form: can swim.
After did/didn't → base form: didn't go.
After have/has/had → third form: have gone.
In the passive → third form: was written.
After enjoy/finish/keep and ANY preposition → -ing.
lesson.watch_out: A bare -ing is not a verb: "we setting our plan" needs are — or must become "we set".
lesson.tip: After a preposition, always -ing — the one rule with no exceptions.

punctuation.rule_a2: Two full sentences cannot join with a comma. Use a full stop: I'm tired. I'll stop.
punctuation.rule_b1: Cover the comma: if both halves are complete sentences, the comma is illegal. Fix with a full stop, a semicolon, a conjunction, or by subordinating one half.
punctuation.bridge: Монгол цэг таслал амьсгааг дагадаг; англи цэг таслал дүрмийг дагадаг. Таслал хоёр бүтэн өгүүлбэрийг холбож чадахгүй.

examples.explanation: Never put a comma between subject and verb.

examples.right: We stopped because it was late.
examples.explanation: 'Because…' alone is not a full sentence — attach it to one.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian commas follow breath and rhythm; English commas follow GRAMMAR. The signature error is the comma splice: two complete sentences joined by a comma — "I'm tired, I'll stop." The test: cover the comma; if both halves are complete sentences, the comma is illegal. Four legal fixes: a full stop, a semicolon, a comma PLUS a joining word (and, but, so), or making one half depend on the other ("Because I'm tired, I'll stop").
lesson.explain_a2: Хоёр бүтэн өгүүлбэрийг таслалаар холбож БОЛОХГҮЙ. "I'm tired, I'll stop" ❌ → "I'm tired. I'll stop." ✅

extra_examples.wrong: The results came back, the score is low.
extra_examples.right: The results came back. The score is low.

extra_examples.wrong: It was late, we kept walking.
extra_examples.right: It was late, but we kept walking.
The tickets were booked on Monday.

how: Cover the comma with a finger.
Read each half alone. Both complete sentences? The comma is illegal.
Fix 1: full stop. Fix 2: semicolon. Fix 3: comma + and/but/so.
Fix 4: make one half depend: Because I'm tired, I'll stop.
lesson.watch_out: 'However' cannot glue sentences with commas — it needs a full stop or semicolon before it.
lesson.tip: Cover-the-comma test: complete sentence + complete sentence → the comma is illegal.

pronoun_gender.rule_a2: he = эрэгтэй, she = эмэгтэй. My wife — she.
pronoun_gender.rule_b1: You know this rule; the error happens at speed because «тэр» never forces the choice. Only timed practice fixes it — not re-reading the rule.
pronoun_gender.bridge: «Тэр» нь he, she, it гурвууланг нь хэлдэг. Энэ бол мэдлэгийн биш, хурдны асуудал.

examples.wrong: My wife, he works in a school.
examples.right: My wife — she works in a school.

examples.wrong: My father, she is a driver.
examples.right: My father, he is a driver.
examples.explanation: «Тэр» splits in English: male → he, female → she.
The possessive carries gender too: her phone, his phone.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian «тэр» covers he, she, it and that — English forces the choice every single time. You already KNOW the rule; the error happens at speed, because your brain never had to make this choice before. That means re-reading the rule does nothing. Only fast, repeated practice makes the choice automatic: describe people around you in three-second bursts — my wife, SHE…; my boss, HE…
lesson.explain_a2: «Тэр» = he (эрэгтэй), she (эмэгтэй), it (юм). Та дүрмийг мэднэ — асуудал нь хурд. Хурдан дасгал л засна.

extra_examples.wrong: My mother, he is a teacher.
extra_examples.right: My mother — she is a teacher.

extra_examples.wrong: My manager is kind. She is a good man.
extra_examples.right: My manager is kind. He is a good man.

how: Female person → she / her. Male person → he / him.
Thing, animal, company → it / its.
Train SPEED, not knowledge: describe people around you in 3-second bursts.
Re-check pronouns in sentence two and three — that's where they slip.
lesson.watch_out: The first pronoun is usually right; the follow-up sentence is where «тэр» strikes. Proofread pronouns separately.
lesson.tip: Speed drill: point at photos, say he/she in under 3 seconds each.

register.rule_a2: To be polite: I'd like… / Could you…? 'I want' sounds too strong.
register.rule_b1: English politeness lives in modal verbs, not pronouns: more words + more distance = more polite. The ladder: I'd like → Could you → Would you mind → I was wondering whether you might.
register.bridge: Та гэж хэлснээр эелдэг байдал монголоор илэрхийлэгддэг. Англид 'you' ганцхан тул эелдэг байдал modal үйл үг рүү нүүсэн. Та бүдүүлэг хэлээгүй — орчуулгад л алга болсон.

examples.wrong: And I want to add a journal.
examples.right: In addition, I'd like to add a journal.
examples.explanation: In formal writing, prefer 'In addition' to starting with 'And'.

examples.right: Could you send me the data?
examples.explanation: Requests use 'Could you…?' — a bare imperative reads as an order.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian politeness lives in the pronoun: та vs чи, one word changes everything. English has no polite "you" — politeness moved into modal verbs and length: more words + more distance = more polite. "I want the report" is not rude in your head — you translated та correctly and the politeness got lost in transit. The ladder: I'd like → Could you…? → Would you mind…? → I was wondering whether you might… For work email, this matters more than perfect grammar.
lesson.explain_a2: Та гэдэг үг англид байхгүй. Эелдэг байдал modal үйл үгэнд байдаг: "I want" ❌ → "I'd like" ✅. Хүсэлт: "Could you…?"

extra_examples.right: Could you send me the meeting notes?

extra_examples.wrong: I want a day off tomorrow.
extra_examples.right: I'd like a day off tomorrow.
Could you give me five minutes?

how: Want something? → I'd like… (not I want).
Need someone to act? → Could you…?
Bigger favour → Would you mind + -ing…?
Email to a boss/client → one step politer than feels natural.
lesson.watch_out: 'Please' alone does not rescue a command — "Please send it" still orders. The magic is in Could/Would.
lesson.tip: More words = more polite. Practise moving one request up and down the ladder.

capitalization.rule_a2: I is always big. Languages too: English, Mongolian. Days: Monday.
capitalization.rule_b1: Capitalise I, languages, nationalities, days and months — small, mechanical, and instantly noticed by any reader.
capitalization.bridge: Монголоор 'би' жижиг үсэгтэй; англиар 'I' үргэлж том. Хэлний нэр ч том үсгээр эхэлдэг.

examples.explanation: 'I' is always capital.
Language names are capitalised: English.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian does not capitalise "би"; English ALWAYS capitalises "I" — alone, mid-sentence, everywhere. Also capitalised: languages and nationalities (English, Mongolian), days (Monday), months (July), and names. Small, mechanical, and instantly visible to any reader — an examiner notices a lowercase "i" before anything else on the page.
lesson.explain_a2: "I" үргэлж том үсгээр. Хэлний нэр, гарагийн нэр, сарын нэр бас том: English, Monday, July.
how: I → always capital, everywhere in the sentence.
Languages, nationalities, days, months, names → capital letter.
Before sending, scan the text once ONLY for capitals.
lesson.watch_out: Seasons stay small (summer, winter), and so do school subjects unless they are languages (maths, but English).
lesson.tip: Before sending anything, scan once just for i / english / monday.

countability.rule_a2: Some words never take -s: information, advice, equipment, news, money, work.
countability.rule_b1: About 15 English nouns are uncountable even though they feel countable: information, advice, equipment, research, evidence, news, work, money. Count them with 'a piece of'.
countability.bridge: Монголд ийм ялгаа байхгүй — цээжлэх жагсаалт: information, advice, equipment, furniture, news, research, evidence, knowledge, progress, work, money, traffic, weather, software, staff.

examples.explanation: 'Equipment' never takes -s.

examples.right: He gave me a piece of advice.
examples.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable: a piece of advice.

lesson.explain_b1: About fifteen English nouns are uncountable even though they FEEL countable: information, advice, equipment, furniture, news, research, evidence, knowledge, progress, work, money, traffic, weather, software, staff. They never take -s and never take "a". To count them, use a container: a PIECE of advice, THREE ITEMS of equipment, a lot of work. "News" looks plural but takes a singular verb: the news IS good.
lesson.explain_a2: Эдгээр үгэнд -s хэзээ ч орохгүй: information, advice, equipment, money, work. Тоолохдоо: a piece of advice.

extra_examples.right: She gave me a lot of advice.

how: Memorise the 15: information, advice, equipment, furniture, news, research, evidence, knowledge, progress, work, money, traffic, weather, software, staff.
Never a/an, never -s with them.
Need to count? Use a container: a piece of advice, an item of equipment, three sums of money.
lesson.watch_out: 'News' looks plural but takes IS. 'Work' (ажил) is uncountable — 'a work' means a work of art.
lesson.tip: Memorise the list of 15 — reasoning will not help; they simply must be known.

determiners.rule_a2: One pointer word only: my report (not 'the my report'). another + ганц тоо: another sample.
determiners.rule_b1: Only one central determiner per noun: 'a my friend' → 'a friend of mine'. 'another' takes a singular noun; 'every' takes a singular noun and verb. its = эзэмшил, it's = it is.
determiners.bridge: Монголоор 'миний энэ тайлан' болно; англиар 'the my report' болохгүй — нэг л заагч үг.

examples.explanation: it's = it is; its = эзэмшил (possessive).
Possessive is 'its' with no apostrophe: its grade.

lesson.explain_b1: English allows only ONE central pointer word per noun: "the my report" is impossible — choose "my report" or "the report". "A my friend" becomes "a friend of mine". "Another" contains "an", so it takes a singular noun: another cup, but OTHER cups. "Every" also takes singular: every student KNOWS. And the apostrophe pair: its = possession, it's = it is.
lesson.explain_a2: Нэг нэр үгэнд нэг л заагч үг: my report (the my report ❌). another + ганц тоо, other + олон тоо. it's = it is; its = эзэмшил.
how: One pointer word per noun: my report OR the report — never both.
another + singular (another cup); other + plural (other cups).
every + singular noun + singular verb: every student knows.
it's = it is; its = эзэмшил. Expand to test: 'it is ready' works → it's.
lesson.watch_out: "a my friend" cannot be repaired with order — it becomes "a friend of mine".
lesson.tip: it's ready = it IS ready. its name = түүний нэр.

collocation.rule_a2: Words go in fixed pairs: make a decision, do research, heavy rain. Learn the pair, not the rule.
collocation.rule_b1: Collocations are fixed partnerships — memorise them as chunks. Verbs that take NO preposition: discuss, enter, approach, marry, lack, mention, answer, reach, join, affect, phone.
collocation.bridge: Үг үгтэйгээ хосоороо явдаг. Монголоос үгчлэн орчуулахад хос эвдэрдэг: 'шийдвэр гаргах' → make (not do) a decision.

examples.explanation: 'Discuss' takes no preposition: discuss it.
explain something TO someone: explain the data to me.

lesson.explain_b1: Words travel in fixed pairs, and the pairs do not survive translation: you MAKE a decision (not do), DO research (not make), rain is HEAVY (not strong), you TURN ON a light (not open). There is no rule — only memory, so learn them as chunks. A special trap list: verbs that take NO preposition at all — discuss, enter, approach, marry, lack, mention, answer, reach, join, affect, phone. "Discuss about it" ❌ → "discuss it" ✅.
lesson.explain_a2: Үгс хосоороо явдаг: make a decision, do research, heavy rain, turn on the light. Дүрэм байхгүй — хосыг цээжил.

extra_examples.wrong: We did a plan for the trip.
extra_examples.right: We made a plan for the trip.

extra_examples.wrong: There was a strong rain last night.
extra_examples.right: There was heavy rain last night.

how: Learn verb + noun as ONE unit: make-a-decision, do-research.
MAKE: decision, mistake, plan, progress, an effort.
DO: research, homework, business, your best.
No preposition after: discuss, enter, marry, answer, reach, phone.
lesson.watch_out: Your instinct will translate the Mongolian pair word-for-word — and be wrong. Trust the memorised chunk, not the feeling.
lesson.tip: Learn verb + noun as one word: "make-a-decision" is one unit.

word_choice.rule_a2: Name the real thing: not 'things', say 'exercises'. good → well after a verb.
word_choice.rule_b1: 'Thing' and 'stuff' are the weakest nouns in English — name the actual noun. Watch participial pairs (interested/interesting) and Russian-loan false friends (магазин ≠ magazine, кабинет ≠ cabinet).
word_choice.bridge: Орос гаралтай зээл үгс англид өөр утгатай: магазин бол shop, magazine биш; кабинет бол office, cabinet биш.

examples.explanation: The teacher TEACHES; the student LEARNS.

examples.wrong: I can talk but not good.
examples.right: I can talk but not well.
examples.explanation: After a verb use 'well', not 'good': speak well.

lesson.explain_b1: Three traps. First, "thing/stuff" — the weakest nouns in English: always name the actual noun ("exercises", not "fitness things"). Second, participial pairs: you are interestED (how you feel); the rock is interestING (what causes the feeling). "I am boring" says you make others sleep! Third, Russian loanwords that shifted meaning in Mongolian: магазин is a shop (not magazine), кабинет is an office (not cabinet).
lesson.explain_a2: "Thing" гэхийн оронд жинхэнэ нэрийг хэл. interestED = сонирхож байгаа хүн; interestING = сонирхолтой юм. Магазин = shop!

extra_examples.wrong: I bought it in a magazine.
extra_examples.right: I bought it in a shop.
We cleaned and checked the data.

how: Caught yourself writing thing/stuff? Stop and name the real noun.
Feeling inside a person → -ed: I am bored / interested / tired.
The cause outside → -ing: The film is boring / interesting.
Russian loanwords: double-check meaning before trusting them.
lesson.watch_out: "I am boring" tells people YOU put them to sleep. One letter, big difference.
lesson.tip: -ED = the person's feeling. -ING = the thing causing it.

modifier_placement.rule_a2: Never put a describing word between the action and the thing: He examined the core carefully.
modifier_placement.rule_b1: Adverbs never sit between verb and object. Frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after 'be'. Adjective order: opinion–size–age–shape–colour–origin–material.
modifier_placement.bridge: Монголоор дараалал чөлөөтэй — дагавар үүргийг заадаг тул. Англиар байрлал өөрөө үүргийг заадаг.

examples.explanation: Adjective order: opinion–size–age–shape–colour–origin–material.
Frequency adverbs go AFTER 'be': I am always careful.

lesson.explain_b1: In Mongolian, word order is free because suffixes mark each word's job; in English, position IS the job. Three placement rules: an adverb never sits between the verb and its object ("read the letter carefully", never "read carefully the letter"); frequency adverbs (always, never, often) go BEFORE a main verb but AFTER "be" ("I always check" / "I am always careful"); adjectives follow the order opinion–size–age–shape–colour–origin–material ("an old black wooden box").
lesson.explain_a2: Үйл үг ба юуг нь хооронд нь үг бүү оруул: read the letter carefully. always/never → үндсэн үйл үгийн ӨМНӨ: I always check.
how: Adverb wants in? Send it to the END or the FRONT — never between verb and object.
always/never/often/usually → BEFORE the main verb: I always check.
…but AFTER be: I am always careful.
Adjectives queue: opinion–size–age–shape–colour–origin–material.
lesson.watch_out: 'Only' changes meaning with position: "Only I saw him" ≠ "I only saw him" ≠ "I saw only him".
lesson.tip: Never between verb and object — that slot is sacred in English.

comparatives.rule_a2: -er and than travel together: bigger than. Short word → -er, long word → more.
comparatives.rule_b1: '-er + than' is one inseparable unit. One syllable → -er; three or more → more; never both ('more taller').
comparatives.bridge: Монголоор харьцуулалт гарах падежээр бүтдэг: надаас өндөр (миний-аас өндөр). Англид 'than' + -er хоёул хэрэгтэй.

examples.wrong: This deposit is more big than that one.
examples.right: This deposit is bigger than that one.

examples.explanation: British English prefers 'different from' ('than' is common in American).
One comparative only: better (never 'more better').

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian compares with the ablative case: "надаас өндөр" (from-me tall). English needs TWO parts that always travel together: -er + than. "Bigger THAN that one" — never "-er" alone, never "more taller" (one comparative only). The length rule: one syllable → -er (deeper), three or more → more (more expensive), two syllables → messy, learn each word. Superlative: the + -est / the most.
lesson.explain_a2: "Надаас өндөр" → taller THAN me. -er болон than хамт явдаг. "More taller" ❌ — зөвхөн нэг харьцуулалт.

extra_examples.wrong: This city is big from that one.
extra_examples.right: This city is bigger than that one.

how: Count the syllables of the adjective.
One → -er + than: deeper than.
Three or more → more … than: more expensive than.
Superlative: the -est / the most. Irregulars: good–better–best, bad–worse–worst.
lesson.watch_out: Never stack: "more bigger" and "most best" are double comparatives — one marker only.
lesson.tip: Short word → -er than. Long word → more … than. Never both.

relative_clauses.rule_a2: Describe after the thing: the hole that we drilled yesterday.
relative_clauses.rule_b1: Mongolian describes before the noun; English describes after it. Build from two simple sentences: I saw a hole. We drilled it yesterday. → I saw the hole that we drilled yesterday.
relative_clauses.bridge: Миний уншсан ном = [я уншсан] ном — тодорхойлолт өмнө нь. Англиар ард нь: the book that I read.

examples.wrong: The yesterday drilled hole was deep.
examples.right: The hole that we drilled yesterday was deep.

examples.wrong: The woman who works here she is very kind.
examples.right: The woman who works here is very kind.
examples.explanation: The relative pronoun IS the subject — don't repeat it with she.

examples.wrong: I know a man which repairs phones.
examples.right: I know a man who repairs phones.
examples.explanation: who = people, which = things, that = both.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian describes BEFORE the noun: "миний уншсан ном" (my-read book). English describes AFTER it: "the book THAT I READ". Build from two simple sentences: "I met a woman. She teaches maths." → "I met a woman who teaches maths." Who = people, which = things, that = both. The professional bonus: reduced relatives drop "that is/was" — "the photos taken yesterday", "the email sent this morning" — the key to clear formal writing.
lesson.explain_a2: Монголоор тодорхойлолт нэрийн ӨМНӨ, англиар АРД нь: the book THAT I read. Хоёр энгийн өгүүлбэрээс эхэл.

extra_examples.wrong: The yesterday arrived equipment is broken.
extra_examples.right: The equipment that arrived yesterday is broken.
The engineer who was helping us left.

extra_examples.wrong: I read the you sent report.
extra_examples.right: I read the report that you sent.

how: Write two short sentences: I met a woman. She teaches maths.
Replace the repeated person/thing with who (people) or which/that (things).
Attach it AFTER the noun: the woman who teaches maths.
Formal writing bonus: drop 'that is/was' — the email sent this morning.
lesson.watch_out: After a comma, 'that' is forbidden — non-defining clauses take which/who: "The report, WHICH arrived late, …"
lesson.tip: Stuck? Write two short sentences first, then join them with that/who/which.

reported_speech.rule_a2: say + words, tell + person: He told me the results. He said the results were good.
reported_speech.rule_b1: Reported speech steps one tense back, keeps statement word order, and distinguishes say (no person) from tell (person first).
reported_speech.bridge: Монголоор «гэж» + шууд яриа, цаг хөрвүүлэлт байхгүй. Англи нэг алхам ухраадаг: is → was.

examples.wrong: She said me she was busy.
examples.right: She told me she was busy.
examples.explanation: A person after the verb → TELL. 'Said me' is impossible.

examples.wrong: He told that he was late.
examples.right: He said that he was late.
examples.explanation: No person mentioned → SAY. The rule runs both ways.

lesson.explain_b1: Three rules. Say vs tell: TELL needs a person ("he told ME"), SAY does not ("he said the price was low") — "he said me" is impossible. Backshift: reporting steps one tense back — "I am tired" becomes "he said he WAS tired". Reported questions lose their inversion and their question mark: "Where do you work?" becomes "He asked where I workED" — statement order, because it is no longer a question.
lesson.explain_a2: tell + хүн: He told ME. say + үг: He said (that)… Асуултыг дамжуулахад дараалал энгийн болно: He asked where I worked.

extra_examples.wrong: He asked where did I study.
He said he is tired yesterday.
extra_examples.right: He said he was tired yesterday.

how: Person mentioned? → TELL: he told ME. No person? → SAY: he said (that)…
Shift the tense one step back: 'I am tired' → he said he WAS tired.
Reported question → statement order, no question mark: he asked where I worked.
Shift time words too: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day.
lesson.watch_out: Still-true facts may keep their tense: "She said the Earth IS round" — backshift is a tool, not a prison.
lesson.tip: Inside a sentence, a question becomes a statement — no inversion, no question mark.

spelling.rule_a2: English spelling does not follow sound. Learn the written word together with how it sounds.
spelling.rule_b1: Cyrillic is nearly phonetic; English spelling is a 500-year-old fossil. Expect errors on words you know perfectly by ear — native speakers misspell too. Never learn a written word without its sound.
spelling.bridge: Кирилл үсэг = нэг үсэг, нэг авиа. Англид тийм биш: through, though, thought — гурван өөр дуудлага.

examples.right: There is a lot to do.
examples.explanation: 'A lot' is always two words.
i before e except after c: believe, receive.

lesson.explain_b1: Mongolian Cyrillic is nearly one letter = one sound; English spelling is a 500-year-old fossil: through, though, thought, tough, thorough — the same -ough, five different sounds. So expect spelling errors on words you know perfectly BY EAR — that is normal, and native speakers misspell too. The practical rule: never learn a written word without its sound, and never learn a heard word without its spelling. They are two separate facts about every English word.
lesson.explain_a2: Англи үгийн бичлэг дуудлагыг дагадаггүй. Шинэ үгийг сурахдаа бичлэг + дуудлага хоёуланг нь хамт сур.

extra_examples.right: We have a lot of work.

how: Learn every new word TWICE: how it sounds + how it is written.
Keep a personal traps list — your five worst words, checked before sending.
In doubt? Look it up. English spelling is memory, not logic.
lesson.watch_out: The classics: a lot (two words) · receive (i before e except after c) · which/witch · their/there/they're.
lesson.tip: i before e except after c: receive, believe. And "a lot" is always two words.

grammar.explanation: Job words need 'a': I am a geologist.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: Job words need 'an' before a vowel sound: an engineer.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.answer: I work in the mining industry.
grammar.explanation: Industry names take 'the': the mining industry.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: A new, countable thing needs 'a': a new deposit.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.answer: The deposit is in the Gobi Desert.
grammar.explanation: Deserts take 'the': the Gobi Desert.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: Country names take no article: in Mongolia.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: Language names take no article: speaks English.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.prompt: I go to the work at 8.
grammar.explanation: Fixed phrase: go to work, no 'the'.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: A subject in general takes no article: Geology is interesting.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: 'Hour' starts with a vowel SOUND, so: an hour.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: 'University' starts with a /j/ sound, so: a university.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.prompt: I saw a rock. A rock was heavy.
grammar.answer: I saw a rock. The rock was heavy.
grammar.explanation: Second mention becomes 'the': we both know which rock now.
grammar.bridge: Монгол хэл тодорхой зүйлийг -ыг/-ийг дагавраар тэмдэглэдэг. Ойлголт нь танд аль хэдийн бий — англи хэл зөвхөн тусдаа үг ашигладаг. (Mongolian already marks definiteness with the accusative suffix; English uses a separate word.)

grammar.explanation: After a number, add -s: three samples. English repeats itself.
grammar.bridge: Гурван ном → three books. Монголд тоо нь олон тоог хэлчихдэг тул -s хэрэггүй; англи давхардуулдаг. Логикгүй ч хүлээн зөвшөөр.

grammar.explanation: 'Information' never takes -s: much information.
grammar.bridge: Монголд ийм ялгаа байхгүй — цээжлэх жагсаалт: information, advice, equipment, furniture, news, research, evidence, knowledge, progress, work, money, traffic, weather, software, staff.

advanced.title: Telling a story: past tenses together
advanced.explain: A story in English uses three past tenses as three camera angles. Past simple is the events, one after another: "She opened the door and saw the letter." Past continuous is the background running behind an event: "I was cooking when she arrived" — the cooking was already in progress, the arrival cut into it. Past perfect reaches FURTHER back, to something before the story: "She had already left when I called" — the leaving happened first. Mongolian tells all three with context; English marks each with its own verb form.
how: Events in order → past simple: opened, saw, said.
Background action interrupted → was/were + -ing: I was cooking when…
Earlier than the story → had + third form: she had already left.
Test: can you draw it? Line = continuous, dot = simple, dot before the line = past perfect.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор "хоол хийж байтал ирсэн" гэдгийг -ж байтал гэсэн нэг хэлбэр илэрхийлдэг. Англид фон (was cooking) ба үйл явдал (arrived) тус тусдаа хэлбэртэй.

examples.right: I was cooking when she arrived.

examples.wrong: When I called, she already left.
examples.right: When I called, she had already left.

examples.wrong: While I was walk home, it started to rain.
examples.right: While I was walking home, it started to rain.

advanced.watch_out: "When" + past simple usually means the event; "while" + past continuous the background. Mixing them flips your story's meaning.
advanced.tip: One line, one dot: background gets -ing, the interruption gets past simple.

quiz.wrong: She watched TV when the phone rang, so she was answering it.
quiz.right: She was watching TV when the phone rang, so she answered it.
quiz.explanation: Background = was watching; events = rang, answered.

quiz.wrong: By the time we arrived, the film started.
quiz.right: By the time we arrived, the film had started.
quiz.explanation: 'By the time' points further back: had + third form.

advanced.title: Verb + verb: -ing or to?
advanced.explain: When two verbs meet, the second one's form depends on the FIRST verb — and there is no logic, only lists. Group 1 takes -ing: enjoy, finish, keep, avoid, suggest, practise, mind ("I enjoy reading"). Group 2 takes to: want, decide, hope, plan, promise, agree, learn ("I decided to leave"). A few take both with different meanings: "stop smoking" = quit; "stop to smoke" = pause in order to smoke. The one reliable rule with zero exceptions: after ANY preposition, always -ing — "interested in learning", "look forward to hearing".
how: Learn the -ing list as a chant: enjoy–finish–keep–avoid–suggest–mind.
Learn the to-list: want–decide–hope–plan–promise–agree–learn.
After a preposition (in, of, at, about, to*): ALWAYS -ing.
Meaning-changers (stop, remember, try, forget): learn each pair as two words.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор "уншиж дуусгах", "унших гэж шийдэх" — дагавар нь ялгадаг. Англид эхний үйл үг нь хоёр дахийнхаа хэлбэрийг шийддэг: жагсаалтыг цээжлэхээс өөр зам байхгүй.

examples.wrong: I enjoy to swim in summer.
He stopped to smoke last year. (= quit)

advanced.watch_out: "Look forward to" ends in the PREPOSITION to, not infinitive to — so it takes -ing: looking forward to seeing you.
advanced.tip: Unsure? Check if a preposition sits before the verb — preposition wins, -ing follows.

quiz.wrong: I suggested to go by train.
quiz.right: I suggested going by train.
quiz.explanation: suggest is in the -ing group: suggest doing.

quiz.wrong: She is good at explain things.
quiz.right: She is good at explaining things.
quiz.explanation: After a preposition (at), always -ing — the no-exception rule.

advanced.title: Must be, might be, can't be — guessing with grammar
advanced.explain: English reuses its modal verbs to show HOW SURE you are about a guess. "The lights are on — he MUST be home" (90% sure, evidence says yes). "He MIGHT/MAY/COULD be in a meeting" (50%, one option among several). "He CAN'T be home — his car is gone" (90% sure the answer is NO). Note the strange pair: the opposite of "must be" is "can't be", not "mustn't be". For past guesses add have + third form: "She must HAVE MISSED the bus."
how: Evidence says YES → must be / must have done.
Just possible → might / may / could be.
Evidence says NO → can't be / can't have done (never 'mustn't be').
Guessing about the past → modal + have + third form.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор "гэртээ байгаа байх", "байж магадгүй", "байх боломжгүй" гэж тусдаа үгсээр хэлдэг. Англид ижил ажлыг modal үйл үгс хийдэг — итгэлийн хэмжээгээр шатласан.

examples.wrong: The lights are on — he should be home, I am 90% sure.
examples.right: The lights are on — he must be home.

examples.wrong: He mustn't be at work, his car is here.
examples.right: He can't be at work — his car is here.
She must have missed the bus.

advanced.watch_out: "Mustn't" means FORBIDDEN, not "surely not". The negative of a must-guess is can't.
advanced.tip: Certainty ladder: must be (yes!) → might be (maybe) → can't be (no!).

quiz.wrong: The office is dark. They mustn't be there.
quiz.right: The office is dark. They can't be there.
quiz.explanation: Negative deduction takes can't, never mustn't.

quiz.wrong: You look tired. You must worked late.
quiz.right: You look tired. You must have worked late.
quiz.explanation: Past guess = modal + have + third form.

advanced.title: Wishes and regrets
advanced.explain: English expresses wishes with a tense shift — the same unreality trick as conditionals. A wish about NOW takes the past: "I wish I HAD more time" (I don't). A regret about the PAST takes past perfect: "I wish I HAD STUDIED harder" (I didn't). Annoyance about a habit takes would: "I wish he WOULD stop calling so late." For advice-flavoured regret, "should have" does the work: "I should have asked earlier."
how: Wish about now → wish + past simple: I wish I knew.
Regret about the past → wish + had done: I wish I had gone.
Complaint about behaviour → wish + would: I wish you would listen.
Self-regret → should have + third form: I should have called.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор "цаг байсан ч болоосой", "явсан бол доо" — болоосой/бол доо хэлбэрүүд. Англид цагийг НЭГ АЛХАМ ухраах нь хүслийг заадаг.

examples.wrong: I wish I have more time.
examples.right: I wish I had more time.

examples.wrong: I wish I studied harder last year.
examples.right: I wish I had studied harder last year.

examples.wrong: I should ask her when I had the chance.
examples.right: I should have asked her when I had the chance.

advanced.watch_out: "I wish I would…" about yourself is impossible — would-wishes aim at OTHER people's behaviour.
advanced.tip: Wish = reality minus one tense step. Now→past, past→past perfect.

quiz.wrong: I wish I know the answer.
quiz.right: I wish I knew the answer.
quiz.explanation: A wish about now steps back to past simple.

quiz.wrong: I wish I didn't sell my bike last year.
quiz.right: I wish I hadn't sold my bike last year.
quiz.explanation: Past regret: wish + had(n't) + third form.

advanced.title: Have it done — when others do it for you
advanced.explain: "I cut my hair" means you held the scissors yourself. When someone does it FOR you, English has a special machine: have/get + thing + third form. "I had my hair cut", "We got the car repaired", "She had her phone fixed". The doer disappears exactly like in the passive; the focus is the arranged service. The same shape with a person after have/get means you arranged for THEM to act: "I had the plumber check the boiler."
how: Service done for you → have/get + THING + third form: had my hair cut.
You arranged a person → have + PERSON + base form: had the plumber check it.
Ask yourself: did I do it with my own hands? No → causative.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор "үсээ засуулсан" гэсэн -уул дагавар яг энэ ажлыг хийдэг! Танд ойлголт нь бий — англи нь have/get + 3-р хэлбэр гэсэн бүтэц.

examples.right: I had my hair cut yesterday at the salon.

examples.wrong: We repaired the car at the garage last week.
examples.right: We had the car repaired at the garage last week.

examples.right: She will have her tooth fixed tomorrow.

advanced.watch_out: Word order carries the meaning: "I had cut my hair" (past perfect, you did it) ≠ "I had my hair cut" (someone else did).
advanced.tip: -уулах/-үүлэх ажиллаж байвал англиар have/get + object + third form.

quiz.explanation: A service done for you: have + thing + third form.

advanced.title: Participle clauses — compression
advanced.explain: Advanced writing compresses two sentences into one by dropping the subject and turning the verb into a participle. "Because we arrived late, we missed the start" → "Arriving late, we missed the start." "The road, which was blocked by snow, stayed closed" → "Blocked by snow, the road stayed closed." Active meaning → -ing; passive meaning → third form. One law governs everything: the hidden subject of the participle MUST be the subject of the main clause, or you produce the famous dangling modifier: "Walking to work, the rain started" makes the rain walk.
how: Same subject in both halves? You may compress.
Active → -ing: Arriving late, we…  Passive → third form: Built in 1950, the bridge…
Check for dangling: WHO does the participle? Must be the main subject.
advanced.bridge: Монголын нөхцөл үйл үг (-ж/-аад: ирж, ирээд) яг ийм шахалт хийдэг — "оройтож ирээд, эхлэлийг алдсан". Танил бүтэц, англи хэлбэр л шинэ.

examples.wrong: Because we arrived late, so we missed the start.
examples.right: Arriving late, we missed the start.

examples.wrong: Walking to work, the rain started.
examples.right: Walking to work, I got caught in the rain.

examples.wrong: Building in 1950, the bridge is old.
examples.right: Built in 1950, the bridge is one of the city's oldest.

advanced.watch_out: The dangling modifier is invisible to the writer and glaring to the reader — always ask WHO is doing the -ing.
advanced.tip: -аад/-ж хэлбэрийн ажлыг англиар participle хийдэг: ирээд → arriving, баригдаад → built.

quiz.wrong: Being tired, the meeting felt endless to finish.
quiz.right: Being tired, I found the meeting endless.
quiz.explanation: The participle's hidden subject must be the main subject — I was tired, not the meeting.

quiz.wrong: Writing in 1990, the report is out of date.
quiz.right: Written in 1990, the report is out of date.
quiz.explanation: Passive meaning (the report was written) takes the third form.

advanced.title: Unreal conditionals
advanced.explain: Mongolian has one conditional form (-вал/-бол); English has four, and the advanced ones use PAST TENSE TO MARK UNREALITY, not past time. "If I had time, I would come" — you do not have time NOW; the past form signals imagination, not history. Third conditional stacks it for lost pasts: "If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train" (we didn't, we missed it). The tense moves one step back from reality: real→present, unreal-now→past, unreal-past→past perfect.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор "цаг байвал очно" гэдэг нэг хэлбэр бүх нөхцөлд ажилладаг. Англиар өнгөрсөн цаг нь БОДИТ БУС гэдгийг заадаг — цаг хугацааг биш.

examples.wrong: If I would have time, I would come.
examples.right: If I had time, I would come.

examples.wrong: If we left earlier yesterday, we caught the train.
examples.right: If we had left earlier yesterday, we would have caught the train.

examples.wrong: If I was you, I take the job.
examples.right: If I were you, I would take the job.

how: Is the situation real or imagined? Imagined → shift the tense back.
Unreal NOW → if + past, would + base: If I had time, I would come.
Unreal PAST → if + had done, would have done.
Formal touch: If I WERE you (not was).
advanced.watch_out: "Would" never enters the if-half. If you typed "if … would", delete the would.
advanced.tip: Never "would" in the if-half. Unreal now → past. Unreal past → had + done, would have + done.

quiz.wrong: If I would know the answer, I would tell you.
quiz.right: If I knew the answer, I would tell you.
quiz.explanation: No 'would' in the if-clause: unreal present takes past tense.

quiz.wrong: If she studied harder last year, she passed.
quiz.right: If she had studied harder last year, she would have passed.
quiz.explanation: Lost past: if + had done → would have done.

advanced.title: The passive voice
advanced.explain: English uses the passive when the doer is unknown, obvious, or less important than the action: "The road was closed", "Mistakes were made". Form: be + past participle, and the object moves to the subject seat. The impersonal passive is the backbone of formal writing: "It is believed that…", "The results are thought to show…". Overusing it makes writing heavy — modern style prefers active where the doer matters.
advanced.bridge: Монгол хэлний -гдах хэлбэртэй ойролцоо, гэхдээ англи passive нь be + 3-р хэлбэр гэсэн ХОЁР үгээр бүтдэг: was closed, is believed.

examples.wrong: The report was wrote by the team.
examples.right: The report was written by the team.

examples.wrong: It believes that prices will rise.
examples.right: It is believed that prices will rise.

how: Move the object to the front: Someone closed the road → The road…
Add be in the right tense: was / is being / has been.
Add the third form: closed, written, taken.
Doer matters? Add by…: …was written by the team. Otherwise drop it.
advanced.watch_out: Verbs without objects (happen, arrive, occur) cannot be passive — "was happened" is impossible.
advanced.tip: happen, occur, arrive never take the passive — they have no object to promote.

quiz.wrong: The window was broke during the storm.
quiz.right: The window was broken during the storm.
quiz.explanation: Passive needs the third form: broken, written, taken.

quiz.wrong: It is believe that the plan will work.
quiz.right: It is believed that the plan will work.
quiz.explanation: Impersonal passive: It is believED / thought / said that…

advanced.title: Hedging — careful claims
advanced.explain: Direct claims sound overconfident in academic and professional English: "This proves the theory" invites attack; "This suggests the theory may be correct" invites agreement. The hedging toolkit: appears to, seems to, suggests, indicates, is likely to, may/might, according to. Mongolian marks the SOURCE of knowledge inside the verb; English must add these separate words, or the writer sounds more certain than they are. Hedging is the skill that separates a good report from a risky one.
advanced.bridge: Монгол хэл мэдээллийн эх сурвалжийг үйл үгэндээ (-жээ, -лаа) тээдэг. Англид тусдаа үгс нэмэх ёстой: appears to, suggests, according to.

examples.wrong: This proves that the method works.
examples.right: This suggests that the method works.
The figures appear to be inaccurate.

examples.wrong: Everyone knows this is the best option.
examples.right: This is widely considered the strongest option.

how: Replace 'proves' with suggests / indicates.
Replace 'is' with appears to be / seems to be / may be.
Name your source: according to X, based on the figures.
Soften totals: 'all' → most, 'never' → rarely.
advanced.watch_out: Don't stack hedges — "it might perhaps possibly seem" reads as having no opinion at all. One hedge per claim.
advanced.tip: Ladder of certainty: proves → shows → indicates → suggests → hints. Choose one step weaker than you feel.

quiz.wrong: The data proves our idea completely.
quiz.right: The data suggests our idea is correct.
quiz.explanation: Academic English hedges: suggests/indicates, rarely 'proves'.

quiz.wrong: The company is definitely hiding something.
quiz.right: The company appears to be withholding information.
quiz.explanation: 'Appears to' makes a strong claim defensible.

advanced.title: Inversion for emphasis
advanced.explain: Starting a sentence with a negative adverb forces question order in the main clause — a written, formal, high-register device: "Never have I seen such results", "Not only did they finish early, they also came in under budget", "Rarely does a plan survive contact with reality". The trigger words: never, rarely, seldom, not only, no sooner, under no circumstances, only then. It is emphasis machinery: use it once per page, not once per paragraph.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор өгүүлбэрийн эхэнд юу ч тавьсан дараалал өөрчлөгддөггүй. Англиар negative үг эхэнд орвол асуултын дараалал үүсдэг.

examples.wrong: Never I have seen such a mess.
examples.right: Never have I seen such a mess.

examples.wrong: Not only they finished early, but also cheaply.
examples.right: Not only did they finish early, but they also finished cheaply.

examples.wrong: No sooner we arrived than it started to rain.
examples.right: No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.

how: Pick the negative opener: Never / Rarely / Not only / No sooner…
Then build a QUESTION shape: auxiliary before subject.
No auxiliary in the sentence? Borrow do/does/did.
Use it for the one sentence per page that deserves a spotlight.
advanced.watch_out: Inversion without the negative opener is just an error — the trigger word must come first.
advanced.tip: Negative opener → borrow the question form: Never HAVE I…, Rarely DOES he…, Not only DID they…

quiz.wrong: Rarely he admits a mistake.
quiz.right: Rarely does he admit a mistake.
quiz.explanation: A negative adverb first forces do-support inversion.

quiz.wrong: Under no circumstances you should sign this.
quiz.right: Under no circumstances should you sign this.
quiz.explanation: 'Under no circumstances' triggers auxiliary-before-subject.

advanced.title: Cleft sentences — controlled focus
advanced.explain: Clefts let English point a spotlight: "It was the BUDGET that killed the project" (not the schedule); "What we need is TIME" (not money). The it-cleft (It was X that…) and the what-cleft (What … is X) do the focusing work that Mongolian achieves with word order and particles. They are also the elegant repair for topic-fronting: the thought behind "About the report…" becomes "What worries me is the report."
advanced.bridge: Монголоор "Тайлан Л асуудал байна" гэж Л-ээр онцолдог. Англиар cleft бүтэц онцолдог: It is the report that worries me.

examples.wrong: The budget killed the project, not the schedule, I emphasize.
examples.right: It was the budget that killed the project, not the schedule.

examples.wrong: We need time is the main thing.
examples.right: What we need most is time.

examples.wrong: About the deadline, that worries me.
examples.right: What worries me is the deadline.

how: Decide what deserves the spotlight.
Spotlight a doer/thing → It was X that/who…
Spotlight a need/feeling → What we need/love/fear is X.
Say it aloud — the stressed word should land on X.
advanced.watch_out: The verb after "What … " is singular: "What we need IS time" (even though 'we' is plural).
advanced.tip: To stress WHO/WHAT: "It was X that…". To stress a need or feeling: "What … is X".

quiz.wrong: The manager made the decision is important here.
quiz.right: It was the manager who made the decision.
quiz.explanation: It-cleft spotlights the doer: It was X who…

quiz.wrong: Patience we need now.
quiz.right: What we need now is patience.
quiz.explanation: What-cleft spotlights the need: What we need is X.

advanced.title: The Germanic–Latin register shift
advanced.explain: English has two vocabularies. Everyday words are Germanic: get, buy, ask for, put off, look into. Their formal twins are Latin: obtain, purchase, request, postpone, investigate. Native professionals shift registers by swapping word families — the grammar barely changes. "We got a lot of stuff and put off the meeting" and "We obtained substantial materials and postponed the meeting" say the same thing to two different rooms. Control of this switch reads as native-level polish in writing.
advanced.bridge: Монголоор албан бичигт хэллэг өөрчлөгддөг шиг англид ҮГИЙН САН солигддог: get → obtain, ask for → request, put off → postpone.

examples.wrong: We got the results and put off the launch. (formal report)
examples.right: We obtained the results and postponed the launch.

examples.wrong: Please look into the problem. (legal letter)
The firm asked for more time. (contract)

how: Writing formally? Hunt the phrasal verbs: put off, look into, ask for.
Swap each for its Latin twin: postpone, investigate, request.
Speaking casually? Reverse the swap — Latin words chill a chat.
Build pairs into your vocabulary: get/obtain, buy/purchase, need/require.
advanced.watch_out: Half-swapped sentences sound strangest of all: "We shall buy the stuff" mixes registers — keep one register per sentence.
advanced.tip: Formal document? Swap the phrasal verb for its one-word Latin twin. Everyday talk? Swap back — 'purchase a coffee' sounds absurd.

quiz.wrong: The committee will look into the issue. (formal minutes)
quiz.right: The committee will investigate the issue.
quiz.explanation: Formal register prefers the Latin verb: investigate.

quiz.wrong: We will purchase some milk on the way home. (chat)
quiz.right: We will buy some milk on the way home.
quiz.explanation: Register works both ways — Latin words sound absurd in casual talk.

dialogues.situation: Two colleagues meet in the morning.

lines.en: Morning, Bold! How are you?
lines.mn: Өглөөний мэнд, Болд оо! Сайн уу?

lines.en: Good, thanks. And you?
lines.mn: Сайн, баярлалаа. Та сайн уу?

lines.en: Not bad. Busy day today?
lines.mn: Гайгүй ээ. Өнөөдөр завгүй юу?

lines.en: Pretty busy — we have a meeting at ten.
lines.mn: Нэлээд завгүй — арван цагт хуралтай.

lines.en: Good luck! See you at lunch.
lines.mn: Амжилт! Үдийн хоолон дээр уулзъя.

lines.en: See you!
lines.mn: Уулзъя!

key_phrases.note: Answer is short: 'Good, thanks. And you?' — nobody gives a real report.
= сайн байна. Very common, friendly.
Casual goodbye between people who meet often.

practice.situation: A colleague says: 'Morning! How are you?' — best reply?

options.why: Short + return the question — that is the whole game.

options.text: I am fine thank you and how are you my friend today.
options.why: Too long and formal — textbook English, not real life.
'How are you?' needs a feeling word, not yes/no.

dialogues.situation: First day with a new team member.

lines.en: Hi, I'm Sarah. I don't think we've met.
lines.mn: Сайн уу, би Сара. Бид танилцаагүй юм шиг байна.

lines.en: Hi Sarah, I'm Bold. I'm an accountant in the finance team.
lines.mn: Сайн уу Сара, би Болд. Санхүүгийн багийн нягтлан.

lines.en: Nice to meet you, Bold. How long have you been here?
lines.mn: Танилцахад таатай байна, Болд. Энд ажиллаад удаж байна уу?

lines.en: About three years. And you? What do you do?
lines.mn: Гурван жил орчим. Та? Ямар ажил хийдэг вэ?

lines.en: I'm the new data engineer. Still finding my feet!
lines.mn: Би шинэ дата инженер. Дасаж л байна!

lines.en: You'll be fine. Let me know if you need anything.
lines.mn: Зүгээр дасна аа. Юм хэрэгтэй бол хэлээрэй.

key_phrases.note: am + an — the two words Mongolian drops. Never 'I accountant'.
= Ямар ажил хийдэг вэ? (NOT 'What is your job?' — this is the natural version)
Say it once, at the first meeting only.

practice.situation: Someone asks: 'What do you do?' — best reply?

options.text: I'm an accountant. I work in finance.
options.why: Job + one detail. Perfect shape.
Missing 'an' — job words need an article.
'Things' says nothing — name the real job.

dialogues.situation: Buying water and asking the price.

lines.mn: Болно оо. Энд уншуулна уу… боллоо. Сайхан өдөр болоорой!

key_phrases.note: Opens ANY question to a stranger. Never start with the bare question.
= Энэ ямар үнэтэй вэ?
'I'll take…' is the natural buying phrase — not 'I want two'.

practice.situation: You want to know the price. Best question?

options.why: Excuse me + the set phrase.

options.text: What is the money of this?

key_phrases.note: THERE IS = байна. The question form for finding anything.
зүүн / баруун тийш эргэх

dialogues.situation: A bad line. THE most important skill for real conversations.

lines.en: Hi, this is Bold from the sales team.
lines.mn: Сайн уу, борлуулалтын багийн Болд байна.

lines.en: Hi Bold. The documents arrive on the… (unclear) …day.

lines.en: Sorry, could you say that again? The line is bad.
lines.mn: Уучлаарай, дахин хэлж өгөхгүй юу? Холбоо муу байна.

lines.en: Sure — the documents arrive on Thursday.
lines.mn: Тэгье — бичиг баримтууд пүрэв гарагт ирнэ.

lines.en: Thursday, got it. Could you speak a little slower, please? English is my second language.
lines.mn: Пүрэв, ойлголоо. Жаахан удаан ярьж болох уу? Англи хэл миний хоёр дахь хэл.

lines.en: Of course, no problem at all.
lines.mn: Мэдээж, ямар ч асуудалгүй.

key_phrases.en: Sorry, could you say that again?
key_phrases.note: Use it PROUDLY. Native speakers say it constantly too.

key_phrases.en: Could you speak a little slower?
key_phrases.note: Nobody minds. It shows confidence, not weakness.
= ойлголоо. Confirms you understood.

options.text: Sorry, could you say that again?
options.why: The single most useful sentence in spoken English.

'What?' alone sounds annoyed. Add sorry + could you.

dialogues.situation: Arranging to meet at the weekend.

lines.en: Hey, are you free on Saturday?
lines.mn: Хөөе, бямбад завтай юу?

lines.en: Saturday… I think so. What did you have in mind?
lines.mn: Бямба… завтай байх аа. Юу бодож байгаа юм?

lines.en: Sounds good. What time works for you?

lines.en: How about one o'clock? We could walk after.
lines.mn: Нэг цагт ямар вэ? Дараа нь алхаж болно.

lines.en: Perfect. If something comes up, I'll text you.
lines.mn: Болно. Ямар нэг зүйл гарвал мессеж бичье.

key_phrases.note: free = завтай. ON + day.
'How about…?' — the softest way to suggest anything.
= Ямар нэг зүйл гарвал… ('comes up', present — no 'will' after if!)

practice.situation: You want to suggest 2 pm. Best way?

options.why: Soft suggestion — leaves room for the other person.

options.text: We will meet at two o'clock.
options.why: A decision, not a suggestion — sounds like an order.

options.text: If you will be free at two, we meet.
options.why: No 'will' after 'if': if you're free at two…

dialogues.situation: A short project meeting; you need to update and disagree politely.

lines.en: Bold, could you give us a quick update on the project?
lines.mn: Болд оо, төслийн талаар товч мэдээлэл өгөхгүй юу?

lines.en: Sure. We've finished the first draft — the final numbers come in on Friday.
lines.mn: Тэгье. Эхний ноорог дууссан — эцсийн тоо баасанд ирнэ.

lines.en: Great. So we can send it to the client on Monday?
lines.mn: Сайн байна. Тэгэхээр даваад захиалагч руу явуулж болох нь ээ?

lines.en: I'm not sure that works, actually — the numbers may not be checked. Could we say Wednesday to be safe?
lines.mn: Бүтэхгүй байж магадгүй — тоог шалгаж амжаагүй байж мэднэ. Аюулгүй талаас нь лхагва гэж тохирох уу?

lines.en: Fair point. Wednesday it is.
lines.mn: Зөв санал. Лхагва болгоё.

lines.en: Thanks. I'll send a short summary after the meeting.
lines.mn: Баярлалаа. Хурлын дараа товч мэдээ явуулъя.

key_phrases.en: I'm not sure that works, actually
key_phrases.note: How natives say NO politely — never a bare 'No, impossible'.
Suggesting a change as a question keeps everyone comfortable.
= Зөв юм байна. Accepting someone's argument gracefully.

practice.situation: You disagree with a date. Best way to say it?

options.text: I'm not sure that works — could we say Wednesday?
options.why: Soft no + alternative = professional disagreement.
Bare 'no' burns goodwill — English wraps disagreement in softeners.
Silence = agreement in meetings. Speak, softly.

dialogues.situation: A new friend asks about your family.

lines.en: Do you have brothers or sisters?
lines.mn: Танд ах дүү бий юу?

lines.en: Yes, one brother and two sisters. And you?
lines.mn: Тийм, нэг ах, хоёр эгч дүү. Та?

lines.en: Just one sister. She lives in Darkhan.
lines.mn: Ганц эгчтэй. Тэр Дарханд амьдардаг.

lines.en: Nice! Do you see her often?

lines.en: Family time is the best time.
lines.mn: Гэр бүлийн цаг хамгийн сайхан.

key_phrases.note: The A1 question machine: Do you have brothers? Do you have time?
he/she + livES — the -s that Mongolian never asks for.
Two words that keep every conversation alive.

practice.situation: Someone asks: 'Do you have brothers or sisters?' Best reply?

options.why: Answer + return the question — conversation is ping-pong.
One word ends the game. Add a detail and 'And you?'

options.text: My family is a difficult and long story from history.
options.why: Too much for small talk — keep A1 answers light.

lines.en: So, what seems to be the problem?
lines.mn: За, юу болоод байна вэ?

lines.en: I have a sore throat and a headache. It started two days ago.
lines.mn: Хоолой өвдөж, толгой өвдөж байна. Хоёр хоногийн өмнө эхэлсэн.

key_phrases.en: I have a sore throat / a headache
key_phrases.note: Illness = I HAVE + a + body problem. Never 'my throat is pain'.
ago = өмнө; the past-simple marker doctors always ask for.
once / twice / three times a day — өдөрт нэг/хоёр/гурван удаа.

'Sick of' means annoyed, not ill! Say 'I feel sick.'

lines.en: Sure. Here we are — that'll be eight thousand.
lines.mn: Тэгье. Ирлээ — найман мянга болно.

lines.en: Keep the change. Have a good day!
lines.mn: Хариултаа аваарай. Сайхан өдөр болоорой!
